publisher: Ministry of Trade and Industry Singapore (MTI, mti.gov.sg)
title: Agreement on Trade in Essential Supplies with New Zealand (AOTES)
date_evidence: Agreement reference page on mti.gov.sg; shows only a last-updated line, no publication date displayed (evergreen)
key_claim: Singapore and New Zealand commit not to impose unnecessary export restrictions on agreed essential supplies including food, fuel, healthcare, chemical and construction products; the agreement was signed on 4 May 2026, entered into force for both sides on 17 July 2026, is to be incorporated into their bilateral free trade agreement, and is described as the world's first legally binding bilateral supply chain resilience agreement.
frame_summary: Singapore presents the agreement as a new legal instrument for supply security, arguing that a binding commitment not to restrict exports is what separates crisis resilience from goodwill.
verbatim_quote: commit not to impose unnecessary export restrictions on agreed essential supplies, including food, fuel, healthcare, chemical and construction products
verbatim_list: It is the world's first legally-binding bilateral supply chain resilience agreement.
The Agreement entered into force for both sides on 17 July 2026.
notes: Reference page rather than a dated release, so carried as evergreen and cited with the access date. The entry-into-force date of 17 July 2026 is stated in the page text and corroborated by the dated New Zealand Government release of the same day. The superlative 'world's first' is the source's own description and is attributed to it in the body.

publisher: New Zealand Government, release by Hon Todd McClay (republished by Scoop, scoop.co.nz)
title: World First New Zealand-Singapore Essential Supplies Agreement Now In Force
key_claim: The Trade and Investment Minister announced the agreement's entry into force at an Auckland ceremony on 17 July 2026 attended by Singapore's Deputy Prime Minister; Singapore commits on fuel, medicines and chemicals and New Zealand on food, and the minister ties the agreement to supply pressure from the escalating Middle East conflict.
frame_summary: The New Zealand Government frames the agreement as insurance bought in response to the Middle East supply shock, securing the imports New Zealand cannot produce in exchange for the food it can.
notes: The same release is on beehive.govt.nz, which returned HTTP 403 to automated fetching on repeated attempts; this verbatim republication, attributed 'Press Release: New Zealand Government', is cited instead and the content is classed Tier 1 on that basis. The release makes no mention of Australia or of any other party joining.

publisher: Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE, mbie.govt.nz)
title: Fuel supply disruption response
date_evidence: Live status page on mbie.govt.nz; displays only a 'Last updated' line, no publication date (evergreen)
key_claim: The government's live response page records that New Zealand has aligned its fuel specifications with Australia's standards to improve supply flexibility and is assessing whether further specification changes could help, and that the country remains in phase 1 of the National Fuel Response Plan 2026.
frame_summary: The ministry treats alignment with Australian fuel specifications as a supply flexibility tool it can extend further, not as a temporary concession to be unwound.
verbatim_quote: aligned fuel specifications with Australia's standards to improve supply flexibility, and we are assessing whether further specification changes could be helpful
verbatim_list: We are currently in phase 1 of the National Fuel Response Plan 2026.
notes: A live page, so carried as evergreen and cited with the access date rather than its last-updated line, which the house date rules treat as an anti-pattern if presented as publication. The page was last updated on 7 August 2026 and still carried the alignment when read on 21 September 2026. The earlier March 2026 decision to accept Australian-specification fuel is outside the recency window and is not cited.

title: Approved products certified overseas
date_evidence: Guidance page on building.govt.nz; displays only a 'Last updated' line, no publication date (evergreen)
key_claim: Plumbing and drainage products certified under the Australian WaterMark scheme are being evaluated for possible recognition in New Zealand, on the ground that Australia has a similar regulatory environment and mandates WaterMark certification for specific products.
frame_summary: The regulator treats Australian certification as a candidate for unilateral recognition because the two regulatory environments are similar enough to trust, rather than as something to be jointly negotiated.
verbatim_quote: Currently, plumbing and drainage products certified under the Australian WaterMark certification scheme are being evaluated for possible recognition
verbatim_list: This is because Australia (which has a similar regulatory environment to Aotearoa New Zealand) mandates Watermark certification for specific plumbing and drainage products.
notes: Live guidance page, carried as evergreen and cited with the access date; last updated 10 August 2026. Evidence that the unilateral route runs beyond fuel.

publisher: New Zealand Government, release by Hon Todd McClay (republished by LiveNews, livenews.co.nz)
title: CER Trade Ministers strengthen Single Economic Market agenda
key_claim: The annual CER Trade Ministers' Meeting in Auckland launched a programme of trans-Tasman business-government collaboration to implement the Australia New Zealand Leadership Forum's proposals to reduce the cost of doing business, covering regulatory coherence and common standards, supply chains, climate adaptation, defence industry, space, innovation and technology; announced a 30% increase in joint trans-Tasman standards under a new agreement between the two national standards bodies; and committed to coordinate regional engagement including CPTPP, RCEP, PACER Plus and AANZFTA.
frame_summary: The two governments present the Single Economic Market as accelerating through a negotiated, business-informed agenda of common standards and coordinated trade engagement.
verbatim_quote: launching a new programme of Trans-Tasman business-government collaboration to implement the Australia New Zealand Leadership Forum's proposals to reduce the cost of doing business between New Zealand and Australia
verbatim_list: Advancing regulatory and standards alignment through a 30 percent increase in Joint Trans-Tasman Standards
notes: The original is on beehive.govt.nz, which returned HTTP 403 on repeated attempts; the Australian minister's statement at trademinister.gov.au could not be fetched either. This verbatim republication, attributed 'Source: New Zealand Government', is cited instead and classed Tier 1 on that basis. The release does not mention a crisis supply or export restriction commitment.

publisher: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ, rbnz.govt.nz)
title: OCR increased by 25 basis points to 2.75%
key_claim: The Monetary Policy Committee raised the OCR to 2.75%; annual CPI inflation rose to 4.1% in the June quarter because of higher fuel prices from the Middle East conflict, while inflation excluding vehicle fuels fell to 2.9%, and global supply chains, refining capacity and trade flows remain disrupted.
frame_summary: The central bank treats the fuel shock as a persistent source of imported inflation serious enough to tighten policy, not as a transitory price spike to look through.
verbatim_quote: Inflation increased to 4.1 percent in the June quarter because of higher fuel prices arising from the conflict in the Middle East
verbatim_list: Excluding vehicle fuels, annual CPI inflation decreased to 2.9 percent in the June quarter.
Global supply chains, refining capacity, and trade flows remain disrupted.
notes: Supplies the quantification of how far the fuel shock reached into the New Zealand economy. The 2.9% ex-fuel figure is from the same release, read on the first fetch; the span is stored in verbatim_list for the quantification audit.

publisher: ORF Middle East (Observer Research Foundation, orfme.org)
title: Asia's Energy Stress: Regional Impact of Hormuz Crisis
key_claim: About 80% of oil and 90% of LNG transiting Hormuz is destined for Asia; in response to the crisis China banned kerosene exports, South Korea capped them and India raised taxes to discourage them, pushing crude-to-diesel and jet spreads from 15 to 20 US dollars a barrel to 50 to 80.
frame_summary: The authors argue that Asian energy security in the Hormuz crisis depends on each economy's reserves, diversification and the export behaviour of regional producers, which exposes importers to decisions taken in other capitals.
verbatim_quote: China, the leading global producer of kerosene has banned all exports, South Korea capped them and India raised taxes to disincentivise them
notes: The single structural anchor, 112 days before the scan date. It is canonical here because it documents the regional export restrictions that give a binding no-restriction commitment its value. Authors Mannat Jaspal and Reem Sagahyroon.

title: The Strait of Hormuz crisis threatened Asia's oil and gas lifeline. Here's how the region is rewriting its energy playbook
date_evidence: August 28, 2026, 8:00 PM ET by Katie Silver
key_claim: The International Energy Agency coordinated the release of 400 million barrels from emergency stocks in March, the largest such intervention in its history, and Asian economies are shifting from just-in-time to just-in-case supply chains while diversifying away from Hormuz.
frame_summary: The piece argues the region is restructuring for resilience after the shock, and that the market has proved more resilient than feared.
notes: Tier 3 corroboration of the region-wide turn to precautionary supply arrangements. Carried as faithful summary rather than verbatim because the host frequently refuses automated fetches, and a quote the provenance gate cannot reach would need an override.
